components.name: Arduino Uno R3
components.function: The brain of the circuit. Runs your sketch, drives output pins HIGH (5V) or LOW (0V), and measures voltages on input pins.
components.science: Inside is an ATmega328P microcontroller — millions of transistors switching at 16 MHz. A digital pin is a transistor switch connecting the pin to 5V or GND. Analog pins use an ADC (analog-to-digital converter) that compares an input voltage against 5V and reports it as a number from 0 to 1023 — each step is about 4.9 millivolts.
components.notes: Pin 13 also drives the onboard 'L' LED. Never connect a pin directly to GND or 5V while it is an OUTPUT — that is a short circuit through the chip.

components.name: LED — Light Emitting Diode
components.function: Turns current into light. Use it to SEE what your code is doing — on, off, blinking, or dimmed with PWM.
components.science: An LED is a semiconductor diode: a junction between two doped materials. When current flows forward across the junction, electrons fall into 'holes' and release their extra energy as photons — light. The energy gap of the material sets the color: red ≈ 1.9eV (~625nm), blue ≈ 2.7eV. Because it is a diode, current only flows one way — reversed, the junction blocks and no light appears.
components.notes: Polarity matters! The longer leg is the anode (+) — wire it toward the pin. The shorter leg is the cathode (–) — wire it toward GND. Reversed = no light. Never connect without a resistor: the LED has almost no resistance of its own once conducting.

components.name: Resistor — 220Ω
components.function: Limits how much current flows. In an LED circuit it is the safety valve that keeps the LED under its 20mA maximum.
components.science: Ohm's Law: V = I × R. Current equals voltage across the resistor divided by resistance. With 5V from the pin, minus ~2V dropped by the LED, the resistor sees 3V: I = 3V ÷ 220Ω ≈ 13.6mA — comfortably under 20mA. Electrons colliding with the resistor's carbon lattice convert the excess energy to heat instead of destroying the LED. The colored bands encode the value: red-red-brown = 2, 2, ×10 = 220Ω.
components.notes: No polarity — either direction works. It limits current for the whole series path, so it can go on either side of the LED.

components.name: Potentiometer — 10kΩ
components.function: A knob your code can read. Turn it and analogRead() reports a number from 0 to 1023.
components.science: Inside is a resistive track with a sliding contact (the wiper). With the outer pins on 5V and GND, the track forms a voltage divider: the wiper picks off a voltage proportional to its position — 0V at one end, 5V at the other, smoothly in between. V_out = 5V × (position). The Arduino's ADC converts that voltage to 0–1023.
components.notes: Outer pins go to 5V and GND (either order — swapping just reverses the knob direction). The middle pin (SIG) is the signal: wire it to an analog pin like A0.

components.name: Pushbutton (momentary)
components.function: A switch your code can read. Pressed = the two sides connect; released = they disconnect.
components.science: Two springy metal contacts sit a fraction of a millimeter apart; pressing forces them together, completing the circuit. But metal contacts BOUNCE — they physically vibrate on impact, connecting and disconnecting dozens of times in a few milliseconds. Your code runs fast enough to see every bounce as a separate press, which is why debouncing (ignoring changes for ~50ms) matters. A 'floating' unconnected input pin picks up radio noise and reads randomly — that is why we use INPUT_PULLUP, which connects an internal ~20kΩ resistor to 5V so the pin reads a solid HIGH until the button pulls it to GND.

specs.contacts: 4 legs — each side pair is internally connected

components.notes: With INPUT_PULLUP wiring (button between pin and GND), the logic is inverted: digitalRead() returns LOW when PRESSED and HIGH when released.

components.name: Photoresistor Module (LDR)
components.function: Senses light level. Bright light = high reading, darkness = low reading on the AO pin.
components.science: The sensor is a Light-Dependent Resistor made of cadmium sulfide. Photons hitting the material knock electrons free, creating charge carriers — so MORE light means LESS resistance (from ~1MΩ in darkness to ~1kΩ in bright light). The module pairs the LDR with a fixed resistor as a voltage divider, so the AO pin's voltage rises and falls with light. This is the same physics as a solar panel, except here light controls conductivity instead of generating power.
components.notes: Wire VCC to 5V, GND to GND, and AO (analog out) to an analog pin like A0. The DO pin is a digital threshold output — we use AO for real measurements.

components.name: NTC Thermistor Module (temperature)
components.function: Senses temperature. The OUT pin voltage changes as the sensor warms or cools.
components.science: NTC means Negative Temperature Coefficient: resistance DROPS as temperature rises. Heat gives the semiconductor's electrons enough energy to jump into conduction — roughly, resistance halves for every 20°C rise (described precisely by the Steinhart–Hart equation). The module's voltage divider converts the changing resistance into a changing voltage your ADC can read. This is the same sensor inside digital thermometers and battery packs that stop charging when hot.
components.notes: Wire VCC to 5V, GND to GND, OUT to an analog pin. Readings are not linear in temperature — for lessons we map the raw 0–1023 value to an approximate °C.

components.name: HC-SR04 Ultrasonic Distance Sensor
components.function: Measures distance by echo — like a bat. Your code sends a ping and times how long the echo takes to return.
components.science: One transducer chirps 8 pulses at 40kHz — sound too high for humans to hear. The sound travels at ≈343 m/s (about 29µs per centimeter), bounces off the nearest object, and returns to the second transducer. The ECHO pin goes HIGH for exactly as long as the round trip took. Distance = (time × speed of sound) ÷ 2 — divide by 2 because the sound travels there AND back. In code: cm = microseconds / 58. Sonar, medical ultrasound, and parking sensors all use this same time-of-flight principle.
components.notes: Wire VCC to 5V, GND to GND, TRIG to a digital output pin, ECHO to a digital input pin. Code: pulse TRIG high for 10µs, then pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH) returns the round-trip microseconds.

components.name: RGB LED (common cathode)
components.function: Three LEDs in one package — red, green, and blue. Mix their brightnesses with PWM and you can make any color.
components.science: Your eye has three kinds of color receptors (cones), roughly tuned to red, green, and blue light. The RGB LED exploits that: it can't make yellow light, but red + green photons hitting your eye together are indistinguishable from true yellow. PWM sets each channel's average brightness: analogWrite(pin, 128) pulses the LED on/off 490 times a second — far too fast to see — so your eye averages it to half brightness. 256 levels × 3 channels = 16.7 million colors, the same math as a screen pixel.
components.notes: COM (the longest leg) goes to GND. Each color leg goes through its own resistor to a PWM pin (~3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11). analogWrite each leg 0–255 to mix colors.

components.name: Micro Servo (SG90)
components.function: A motor that moves to the exact angle you ask for, 0–180°, and holds it. Robots, steering, and camera mounts are built from these.
components.science: Inside is a DC motor, a gearbox, a potentiometer, and a control circuit — a complete feedback loop. The pot measures the horn's current angle; the circuit compares it to the angle you requested and drives the motor until they match. That is closed-loop control, the core idea of robotics. Your request arrives as a pulse every 20ms: a 1ms pulse means 0°, 2ms means 180°. The Servo library generates those pulses for you — servo.write(90) sends 1.5ms pulses.
components.notes: Brown/black wire → GND, red → 5V, orange/yellow (signal) → any digital pin. In code: #include <Servo.h>, myServo.attach(pin), myServo.write(angle).

components.name: DC Motor
components.function: Spins continuously — fans, wheels, pumps. Speed follows the average voltage you give it, which is exactly what PWM provides.
components.science: Current through the motor's coil creates a magnetic field that pushes against permanent magnets, spinning the shaft; a commutator flips the current direction every half turn so the push never stops. Physics to respect: a motor is mostly wire, so it draws FAR more current than an Arduino pin's 40mA limit — real builds put a transistor between pin and motor as an electronic valve. And when a spinning motor is switched off, its collapsing magnetic field generates a reverse voltage spike (back-EMF) — a flyback diode across the motor absorbs it. The simulator forgives both so you can focus on the code.

specs.stallCurrent: hundreds of mA — never drive directly from a pin in real life

components.notes: One terminal to a PWM pin (via a driver transistor in real builds), the other to GND. analogWrite(pin, 0–255) sets speed.

components.name: Piezo Buzzer
components.function: Makes sound. Send it a frequency with tone() and it plays that pitch; noTone() stops it. Great for alarms, feedback beeps, and simple melodies.
components.science: Inside is a thin disc of piezoelectric ceramic bonded to a metal plate. Piezo materials flex when a voltage is applied — apply a voltage, the disc bends; remove it, the disc springs back. Drive it with a square wave that switches thousands of times per second and the disc vibrates, pushing air into sound waves you hear as a tone. The pitch is set purely by how fast you toggle the voltage: 440 times a second (440 Hz) is a musical A, 2000 Hz is a shrill beep. tone(pin, freq) generates that square wave in the background so your loop() keeps running; tone(pin, freq, duration) plays for a set number of milliseconds then stops itself. Because a piezo moves almost no current, you can drive it straight from a pin — no resistor needed.

specs.current: a few mA — safe to drive directly from a pin

components.notes: Wire the + terminal (pin 1) to a digital pin and the – terminal (pin 2) to GND. Play a pitch with tone(pin, frequency); stop it with noTone(pin). tone(pin, freq, ms) auto-stops after ms milliseconds. Orientation is forgiving in the simulator.

components.name: LCD Display — 16×2 characters
components.function: Shows two lines of 16 characters — your project's face to the world, no computer required.
components.science: Each character cell is a 5×8 grid of liquid crystal pixels. Liquid crystals twist polarized light; applying a voltage untwists them, blocking the light path and making a dark pixel. The onboard HD44780 controller chip stores a font of 5×8 patterns for every printable character, so your Arduino only sends character codes, not pixels. Data travels over a 4-bit parallel bus: each byte is split into two 4-bit halves clocked in by the E (enable) pin, while RS tells the controller whether the byte is a command or a character.
components.notes: Power: VSS→GND, VDD→5V, V0 (contrast)→GND, RW→GND, backlight A→5V and K→GND. Signals: RS, E, D4–D7 → six digital pins matching LiquidCrystal(rs, en, d4, d5, d6, d7) in code.
components.terminals: VSS, VDD, V0, RS, RW, E, D4–D7, A, K

components.name: DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor
components.function: Measures air temperature AND relative humidity, and reports both back over a single data wire. You talk to it through the DHT library: dht.readTemperature() gives degrees Celsius, dht.readHumidity() gives percent moisture in the air.
components.science: Two sensing elements share one little blue package. Humidity is read by a capacitor whose plastic film soaks up water vapour — as the air gets damper the film holds more moisture, changing how much charge the capacitor stores. Temperature is read by a thermistor, a resistor whose resistance falls as it warms. A tiny chip inside measures both, converts them to digital numbers, and shoots them out on the single DATA pin as a precisely-timed train of pulses. That timing is far too fast and fussy to decode by hand, so you install the DHT library once and it does the bit-banging for you — you just call readTemperature() and readHumidity(). Because the sensor samples slowly, you should only ask it for a new reading about once per second.
components.notes: Wire VCC→5V, GND→GND, and DATA→any digital pin. In code: create the object with DHT dht(pin, DHT11); call dht.begin() once in setup(); then read with dht.readTemperature() and dht.readHumidity(). Don't poll faster than once a second or the readings go stale.
components.terminals: VCC (5V), SDA/DATA (to a digital pin), NC (unused), GND

components.name: Infrared Receiver (38 kHz)
components.function: Listens for the invisible infrared light a remote control flashes at it and turns that flicker into a clean digital signal your Arduino can read. The IRremote library decodes the pulse train into a single command number for whichever button was pressed.
components.science: A remote's LED doesn't glow steadily — it flickers on and off about 38,000 times a second, and that fast flicker is switched in longer and shorter bursts to spell out a number in binary (the NEC protocol). This little receiver has a photodiode tuned to 38 kHz and a demodulator chip that ignores ordinary room light and sunlight (which don't flicker at that rate) and passes only the 38 kHz bursts. It hands the Arduino a stream of clean HIGH/LOW pulses on its OUT pin. Decoding the exact widths of those pulses by hand would be maddening, so you install the IRremote library once: each pass through loop() you ask IrReceiver.decode(), and if a full code has arrived it fills in IrReceiver.decodedIRData.command with the button's number.

specs.range: up to ~8 m, line of sight

components.notes: Three pins: DAT (signal → any digital pin), VCC → 5V, GND → GND. In code: #include <IRremote.hpp>, #define IR_RECEIVE_PIN 7, then IrReceiver.begin(IR_RECEIVE_PIN, ENABLE_LED_FEEDBACK) in setup(). Each loop: if (IrReceiver.decode()) { read IrReceiver.decodedIRData.command; IrReceiver.resume(); }.
components.terminals: DAT (to a digital pin), VCC (5V), GND

components.name: Infrared Remote Control
components.function: The handheld transmitter — a grid of buttons that beam commands to the receiver. Every key flashes an infrared LED with its own unique pattern of pulses, so the board can tell exactly which button you pressed. There are no wires: the signal travels through the air as invisible light.
components.science: Press a key and a tiny microcontroller inside drives an infrared LED, flickering it at 38 kHz and chopping that carrier into a burst pattern that encodes an 8-bit address plus an 8-bit command (the NEC protocol). Different keys send different command bytes — power is 0xA2, the number 1 is 0x30, and so on. Infrared sits just past the red end of the spectrum, so your eyes can't see it, but the receiver's photodiode can. Because it's light, it only works in line of sight and gets swamped if you point two remotes at once.
components.notes: Not wired into the circuit — just drop it on the canvas and click its keys while the sketch runs. Each key sends a command byte (power = 0xA2, 1 = 0x30, …) that shows up in IrReceiver.decodedIRData.command.

components.name: Stepper Motor (4-wire)
components.function: A motor that moves in exact, countable increments instead of spinning freely. Energize its four coils in the right order and the shaft snaps forward one precise step; reverse the order and it steps back. Because every step is the same tiny angle, you can command it to an exact position — no feedback sensor needed — which is why 3D printers, camera rigs, and clocks use them.
components.science: Inside are two coil pairs (A and B) surrounding a toothed magnetic rotor. When you push current through a coil it becomes an electromagnet and tugs the nearest rotor tooth into alignment. By switching current between the coils in a fixed sequence — A+, then B+, then A−, then B− — you drag the rotor around one notch at a time. A common motor has 200 steps per revolution, so each step is 360°/200 = 1.8°. The Arduino Stepper library hides the switching pattern: you tell it stepsPerRevolution and the four control pins in the constructor, call setSpeed(rpm) to choose how fast, and then step(n) to advance n steps (negative n runs it backwards). step() is blocking — it doesn't return until the move finishes.

specs.driver: needs a ULN2003 or H-bridge in real hardware
specs.holding: stays locked in place while a coil is energized

components.notes: Four coil wires: A− A+ B+ B−. In code: #include <Stepper.h>, then Stepper myStepper(stepsPerRevolution, p1, p2, p3, p4); the four pins must match how the coils are wired. Call myStepper.setSpeed(rpm) once, then myStepper.step(steps). A real stepper can't be driven straight from Uno pins — it needs a driver board — but the simulator wires it directly so you can focus on the code.
components.terminals: A- , A+ , B+ , B- (each to a digital pin, via a driver in real life)

components.name: Shift Register (74HC595)
components.function: A chip that turns three Arduino pins into eight outputs. You clock eight bits into it one at a time, then flip a latch and all eight outputs update at once. When you run out of pins for LEDs, seven-segment digits, or relays, a shift register buys you eight more for the cost of three — and you can chain several to get 16, 24, 32… outputs from the same three wires.
components.science: Inside are eight flip-flops in a row — a bucket brigade for bits. Each rising edge on the shift clock (SH_CP) pushes the bit currently on the data line (DS) into the first flip-flop and shoves every other bit one seat down the line. After eight clock pulses your byte is lined up inside, but the outputs haven't moved yet: they follow a second set of latch registers. A rising edge on the latch clock (ST_CP) copies all eight bits to the outputs Q0–Q7 simultaneously, so they change cleanly instead of flickering as you shift. Two active-low housekeeping pins finish the job: MR (master reset) must be HIGH (tie to 5V) or the register stays cleared, and OE (output enable) must be LOW (tie to GND) or the outputs stay off. Arduino's shiftOut(dataPin, clockPin, bitOrder, value) does the eight data-and-clock pulses for you; you wrap it in digitalWrite(latchPin, LOW) … digitalWrite(latchPin, HIGH) to latch the result.

specs.outputs: Q0–Q7, plus Q7' for daisy-chaining more registers
specs.voltage: 2–6 V logic; ~35 mA total across all outputs

components.notes: Three control lines do all the work: DS→a digital pin, SH_CP→a digital pin, ST_CP→a digital pin. Power with VCC→5V and GND→GND; tie MR→5V and OE→GND so the chip is enabled. In code, latch LOW, shiftOut(dataPin, clockPin, MSBFIRST, value), latch HIGH. The simulator shows the eight Q outputs as on-board indicator lights so you can watch your byte appear; on a real board you'd wire Q0–Q7 to eight LEDs (each through its own resistor).
components.terminals: DS, SH_CP, ST_CP (to digital pins) · MR→5V · OE→GND · VCC→5V · GND→GND

components.name: BNO055 9-axis IMU (Adafruit)
components.function: A single chip that knows which way it is pointing. It packs three sensors — an accelerometer (which way is down, plus any shove), a gyroscope (how fast it is spinning), and a magnetometer (a compass) — and a small processor that fuses all nine readings into one clean answer: the board's heading, roll, and pitch, in degrees, updated a hundred times a second. Point it, tilt it, spin it, and it tells you exactly how. This is the sensor that lets a drone hold level, a phone rotate its screen, and a self-balancing robot stay upright.
components.science: Nine 'axes' = three sensors, three axes each. The MEMS accelerometer measures acceleration in m/s^2 on X, Y, Z; sitting still it reads Earth's gravity (~9.81 m/s^2) pointing down, so from its direction you can work out tilt. The gyroscope measures angular rate in degrees/second on each axis — it sees rotation, not position, so it is zero when the board is held still. The magnetometer measures the Earth's magnetic field in microtesla to find true heading. Raw accel is noisy and gyro drifts, so the BNO055's built-in ARM Cortex-M0 runs a sensor-fusion algorithm that blends all three into a stable absolute orientation (Euler angles or a quaternion). The Adafruit_BNO055 library talks to it over I2C at address 0x28: bno.begin() starts it, then sensors_event_t event; bno.getEvent(&event); fills event.orientation.x/.y/.z (heading/roll/pitch in degrees). Pass a vector type — bno.getEvent(&event, Adafruit_BNO055::VECTOR_ACCELEROMETER) — to read event.acceleration or event.gyro instead.

specs.fusion: on-chip ARM Cortex-M0 — absolute orientation, no math on the Uno
specs.output: Euler angles (deg), quaternion, accel (m/s^2), gyro (deg/s), mag (uT)

components.notes: Four wires: VIN->5V, GND->GND, SDA->A4, SCL->A5 (A4/A5 are the Uno's fixed I2C pins). In code: #include <Adafruit_Sensor.h> and <Adafruit_BNO055.h>, then Adafruit_BNO055 bno = Adafruit_BNO055(55, 0x28, &Wire); guard bno.begin() so you know it was found. The gyroscope reads ~0 while the board is still — it senses turning, not tilt; use the accelerometer or the fused orientation for angle.

components.name: Raspberry Pi — Single-Board Computer
components.function: A full Linux computer on one board. Its 40-pin GPIO header lets Python turn real pins HIGH or LOW, read buttons, and make PWM — the same electronics you learned on the Arduino, now driven by Python instead of a compiled sketch.
components.science: The GPIO pins connect to a Broadcom SoC (system-on-chip). Under the RPi.GPIO library, 'BCM' numbering names each pin the way the chip does (GPIO17, GPIO27, …) rather than by its physical header position. A pin set as an output is a transistor switch tying it to 3.3V (HIGH) or 0V (LOW). The Pi has no analog-to-digital converter and its logic level is 3.3V, not 5V — so unlike the Uno, you never feed a Pi input pin more than 3.3V.
components.notes: The header carries 3V3, 5V, GND, and GPIO pins. Drive LEDs from a GPIO pin through a resistor to a GND pin. Never connect 5V to a GPIO input — the pins are only 3.3V tolerant. There is no analogRead here: GPIO pins are digital in/out (with PWM), not analog.
components.terminals: 40-pin GPIO header: 3V3, 5V, GND ×8, and BCM GPIO2–GPIO27.
